title: Sharper than a sword
hookLine: the devotees' way is unique, sharper than a sword and finer than a hair (Anand 14)

cards: A child walks along a curb like a balance beam. Arms out, one foot in front of the other, eyes fixed ahead, while everyone else just walks on the sidewalk. One wobble and she's off.

It takes total attention, and it's strangely absorbing. Now imagine the curb gets thinner, sharp as a blade, fine as a single hair, and someone tells you this, not the wide sidewalk, is the path of those who love God.
That's the fourteenth pauri of Anand Sahib.

teach.b: It opens: bhagtaa kee chaal niraalee. The way of the devotees is unique. Niraalee means distinct, set apart, one of a kind.
Then, in paraphrase: they walk a hard path.
They give up greed, grasping, ego and craving, and they don't talk too much. Then the well-known image: khanniahu tikhee vaalahu nikee, et maarag jaanaa.
Sharper than a double-edged sword, finer than a hair: that is the path they walk. Those who, by the Guru's grace, let go of self, their desire merges into the Lord.
Says Nanak, the way of the devotees, age after age, is unique. Two details stand out. First, khanniahu, from khanda, the double-edged sword.
Guru Amar Das was reaching for an everyday picture of sharpness.

More than a century later, in 1699, a khanda would stir the amrit at the first Khalsa initiation, and today it stands at the center of the Sikh emblem, so Sikhs now hear this line with that blade in mind.
Second, the list of what's given up: greed, grasping, ego, craving, and then, almost funny in its plainness, talking too much.

teach.h: SHARPER THAN A KHANDA, FINER THAN A HAIR.
teach.b: Not some great austerity. Just fewer words. The path isn't hard because it's exotic.
It's hard because it's narrow. Every day brings a hundred small chances to step off: a greedy thought, a proud word, one more thing to grab.
The devotee's way is to stay on the line, again and again, and the ones who do, the pauri says, have let go of self by the Guru's grace.

how: Many Sikhs recite this pauri as part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem, and the khanda, the double-edged sword it names, is used to stir the amrit at the Khalsa initiation.

o: a steep mountain road to a shrine
a sharp word spoken in anger

games.q: the narrow way — tap the pairs.
p: on the list of things given up

s: the pauri says the devotees' path is wide and easy
sharper than a double-edged sword, finer than a hair.
among the things given up in the pauri is talking too much
greed, grasping, ego, craving, and too many words.
the khanda is used to stir the amrit at the Khalsa initiation
the same double-edged sword the pauri names as the measure of the path's sharpness.

games.q: you want to walk the way of the devotees. according to pauri fourteen, what is that path like?
o: wide and comfortable, open to any pace.
sharper than a double-edged sword, finer than a hair.
games.why: khanniahu tikhee vaalahu nikee: sharper than a khanda, finer than a hair. and walked by letting go of self, by the Guru's grace.

practice: If you can stand, find a line on the floor, a floorboard seam or the edge of a rug, and walk slowly along it, heel to toe, for a few steps, saying Waheguru with each one if you pray; if you can't stand, trace a line slowly with one finger.
Notice the attention it takes, and how the mind goes quiet when it has one thing to do. Then sit and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Khanniahu tikhee, sharper than a double-edged sword. Vaalahu nikee, finer than a hair: the devotees' way, walked by letting go of self.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sharper than a double-edged sword, the opening of Anand's most well-known image.

carryVoice: Your line: the narrow way. Even one word left unsaid is a step along it. Day three hundred ninety, done.
